hops.title: Adult canaries hinted that radial cells make neurons
hops.text: Adult canaries keep making new projection neurons for the song-control pathway, and the new cells replace older ones; species and seasonal comparisons suggested a link to learning. In 1990 Arturo Alvarez-Buylla, Marga Theelen and Fernando Nottebohm mapped tritiated-thymidine-labeled cells in the walls of the adult canary's lateral ventricles. The labeled cells bunched into hot spots that matched regions rich in radial cells and the sites where new neurons originate. Smears from those hot spots showed the radial cells themselves taking up the label and dividing. The authors suggested that radial cells give rise to the new neurons, about ten years before the rodent work above.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A bright yellow canary singing on a blossoming spring branch.
image.caption: Dividing radial cells in adult canary brains pointed to a source of new neurons a decade before rodent proof.

hops.title: A human gene folds a marmoset's smooth cortex
hops.text: Common marmosets are small monkeys with a naturally smooth cortex. Humans carry a gene no other living primate has, ARHGAP11B, which began as a partial copy of an older gene, ARHGAP11A. A single C-to-G change in the copy created a new splice site, so 55 nucleotides drop out of the mRNA, the reading frame shifts, and the protein ends in a new tail. In 2020 Michael Heide, Wieland Huttner and colleagues studied fetal marmosets expressing the human gene under its own human promoter. Outer (basal) radial glia increased in the outer subventricular zone, upper-layer neurons increased, and the cortex grew larger and folded.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small common marmoset with white ear tufts perched curiously on a mossy branch.
image.caption: A human-specific gene added outer radial glia in fetal marmosets, and their smooth cortex grew and folded.

hops.title: Rhesus cortical progenitors divide more slowly than a mouse's
hops.text: A rhesus monkey's neocortex is about 100 times larger than a mouse's, so a reasonable guess is that its progenitors divide faster. In 1998 David Kornack and Pasko Rakic timed ventricular-zone progenitors in fetal rhesus monkeys and found the reverse. Against the mouse's 8 to 18 hours, the monkey cycle took about 23 hours at embryonic day 40 and about 54 hours at day 60, up to five times longer. The monkey wins on time instead. Its cortical neurogenesis lasts about 60 days against the mouse's 6. By the authors' estimate, days 40 to 80 alone fit about 28 rounds of division; the whole mouse window fits about 11.

sources.citation: Kornack & Rakic, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 95:1242-1246 (1998)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A calm rhesus macaque beside a tall clock while a tiny mouse runs past a pocket stopwatch.
image.caption: Rhesus progenitors divide more slowly than mouse progenitors but keep neurogenesis running ten times longer.
